Md Mostafa Kamal, Advocate—For the Convict-Petitioner.
Md Mahmudul Hasan, Advocate—For the Complainant-Opposite Party No. 2.
Syed Bashir Hossain Chowdhury, AAG—For the State, Opposite Party No. 1.
parties:
Anwara Khatun ------- Convict-Appellant
vs
State and another ----- Respondents
full_judgment:
10. In contrary, Mr Md Mahmudul Hasan, learned Advocate for the complainant-respondent-opposite Party No.2, vehemently opposes the said submissions as advanced by the learned Advocate for the convict-appellant-petitioner contending that the section 101 of the Evidence Act has shifted the all burden upon the complainant to prove its own case. And to that extent the complainant-respondent opposite party has been perfectly able to prove the case, even he by adducing himself as PW-1 has placed the case properly by producing necessary documents; as because, there has been no legal bar about to prove the complainant's case by adducing and producing single witness. Learned Advocate for the complainant opposite party to that extent referring to section 134 of the Evidence Act submitted that number of witness is not required to prove a case; because, even if a solitary witness has been able to prove the case upon placing trustworthy evidence and to that effect due to the cause of a solitary witness, a judgment cannot be said to be null and void. Learned Advocate for the complainant therefore in support of his said submission referred to the case of Shishir Kanti Pal and others vs Nur Mohammad and others, reported in 55 DLR (AD) 39. He also referring to section 167 of the Evidence Act submitted that no material evidence or improper admission or rejection of evidence is not a ground for reversing the decision of a case and if that is so, this Court itself has the power to examine the evidences as has been adduced and produced in the case which are very much with the LCR and to make a proper decision this Court itself may have to examine the same again. He then referred to a decision of our Apex Court, as has been passed in the case of Md Abul Khair Shahin, vs Emran Rashed and another reported in 28 BLT (AD) (2020) 40 and to that extent he submitted that where the amount promised shall depend on some other complementary facts or fulfillment of another promise and if any cheque is issued on that basis, but that promise is not fulfilled it will not create any obligation on the part of the drawer of the cheque or any right which can be claimed by the holder of the cheque, in due course. He to supplement the said argument submitted that the section 138 of the NI Act, 1881 since did not disqualify any cheque, as such, the cheque in question as used herein cannot be said to be a questionable cheque. He also referring to section 118 of the NI Act, 1881 submitted that it is well founded presumption that every negotiable instrument as made or drawn for consideration and that every such instrument when has been accepted endorsed, negotiated or transferred, will be deemed to have been accepted, endorsed negotiated and transferred for consideration. Thus, the learned Advocate for the complainant opposite party argued that the presumption as laid down in section 118 of the NI Act has certainly goes against the petitioner; as because, she admittedly has given the cheque in question to the complainant opposite party by putting her signature thereto for making repayment of the complainant's loan money who had also got chance in the trial court below to rebut the complainant's claim as made in the case but she failed to do so and now she cannot re-open the same again invoking the revisional Jurisdiction. Learned Advocate therefore urged to discharge the rule upon rejecting the applications as have been filed by the learned Advocate for the convict appellant petitioner. 

 17. The above such claim of the complainant-opposite party and disclaim of the accused-petitioner has not been properly addressed and taken into consideration by the learned judge of the trial Court and later the learned judge of the appellate Court below, also; even though the appellate court is the last Court of fact. But both the court below ignoring the said defence case as of non-considering the very admitted fact of repayment of Taka 1,00,000 to the complainant-respondent and also the defective consideration, however, both the Court kept them silent on that prevailing facts of the case. The trial Court below was though stated the said fact of repayment in the body his judgment but later on did not mention anything in his finding about deducting the said amount from the complainant's claim. The learned Judge of the Appellate Court also was very much silent on the said admitted fact as well as on the defnece plea as agitated in the grounds of the memo of appeal. Thus, certainly a presumption comes to the light that why a lady school teacher aged about 58 years old took Taka 15,00,000 (fifteen lacs), in one bundle, from the complainant by making a promise to make repayment of the same within a short period of only 20 (twenty) days? That presumption has not been taken into consideration by the trial Court and later the appellate Court as well who is being the last Court of fact has to address the same but has ignored the same, definitely. Moreover, the legal notice as claimed to has been served in the case upon the accused-petitioner but that has not been fulfilled the provisions as laid down in section 138 of the NI Act, 1881. As because, by giving 15 (fifteen) days notice the complainant has asked the petitioner to make the payment thereto; whereas, the law provides in this regard 30 (thirty) days notice time. That contradiction has also not been addressed and considered by the court below in the case in hand and certainly that burden of proof goes to the complainant himself first who has failed to perform his duty to do the same. Although he clearly stated in the complaint-petition that the accused petitioner took the amount of Taka 15,00,000 (fifteen lacs) from him, in one bundle which was happened in front of some of the witnesses whose names he clearly mentioned in the complaint-petition. But none of them were produced before the trial Court below to prove the said presumption. It also appears from the trend. of cross examination that a blank cheque without a consideration was given to the complainant by the accused petitioner by putting her signature thereto for securing the loan amount of Taka 1,77,000 (one lac seventy seven thousand) only as she claimed. But the complainant later on upon filling up the same and inserting therein an amount of Taka 15,00,000 (fifteen lacs) has used the said cheque for initiating the pr6ent criminal case against an aged lady school teacher who has no cause to take the said huge amount in one bundle. Can we hold the said solitary testimony of PW-1 as trustworthy evidence without having any supporting evidence thereto for awarding a conviction? Certainly not Section 134 of the Evidence Act, does not say so. 

 18. It also reveals from the cheque in question (Exhibit-2) from which it clearly appears that the amount of the cheque and the name of the complainant as written thereon was not written by same hand but has done by another hand instead of the handwriting of the signature as put therein and the date of the said cheque was also written by separate hand. Those apparently appears were written by other person in separate hands. It also reveals from the record that there are two money receipts wherein the complainant opposite party by putting his signatures on the revenue stamps had received Taka 1,00,000 (one lac) from the accused-petitioner. But the learned judges of the Court below did not take those admitted fact in their consideration while they decided the case in hand. Thus, there has been a clear apprehension that the defence case as was placed has not been properly addressed or considered and the grounds of appeal had also not been addressed properly by the appellate court as well. And further that the presumption of blank cheque and the defective consideration has not been disproved from the side of complainant-opposite party by adducing supporting evidence; although he cited some witnesses name in the complaint petition to support his claim and therefore the said burden of proof certainly goes to the complainant himself but he failed to rebut the same. 

 22. In the instant case the complainant opposite party has cited 4 (four) witnesses name in the complaint petition, saying that the amount as he claimed to have been given loan to the accused petitioner was held in front Of those persons and thus it was his obligation to produce them before the trial court about to proof of his assertion made and also the presumption of defective consideration as raised by the accused-petitioner. If so, they would come in front of the Court, as per section 114(g) of the Evidence Act, they may not support the complainant's claim. But neither the trial Court nor the appellate Court has gone through into the said issue as raised on behalf of the accused petitioner. Even then both the Court below by making a decision in general manner held that the complainant being a trust worthy witness he has been able to prove that the cheque in question was issued and the same was dishonoured and thus, the accused appellant petitioner is liable to be punished for making non-payment of the said cheque's money. That decision of both the Courts below has caused an error in the decision occasioning failure of justice. The appellate Court being the last Court of fact, it was his obligation to address each and every ground as taken in appeal and, as such, he could not ignore the presumption of defective consideration as raised in appeal by the convict-appellant-petitioner. 

 "When a presumption is rebuttable, it only points out that the party on whom lies  the duty of going forward with evidence, on  the fact presumed and when that party has produced evidence fairly and reasonably  tending to show that the real fact is not as  presumed, the purpose of the presumption is  over. To rebut the statutory presumptions as accused is not expected to prove his defence beyond reasonable doubt as is expected of the complainant in a criminal trial. The accused may adduce direct evidence to prove that the cheque in question was not supported by consideration. However, the Court need not insist in every case that the accused should disprove the non-existence of consideration and debt by leading direct evidence because the existence of negative evidence is neither possible nor contemplated. At the same time, it is clear that bare denial of the passing of consideration apparently would not serve the purpose of the accused. Something which is probable has to be proof shifted to the complainant. The burden of proof of the accused to disprove the presumption under sections 118 and 138 of the Act is not so heavy. The preponderance of probability through direct or substantial evidence is sufficient enough to shift the onus to the complainant. Inference of preponderance of probabilities can be drawn from the materials on record and also by reference to the circumstances upon which the party relies." 

 "It is obvious in any case, that the burden of proving the case lay upon the plaintiff, Pirbhu Dayal. We cannot concede in favour of the appellant that any admission, which was made by the defendant regarding .the putting of a signature or a thumb-mark on the document in question, amounted to such an admission of execution as to thrust the burden of proving the case upon him. Obviously, there was no admission of execution of the document, upon which the plaintiff relied, when the defendant stated that he had put his signature and his thumb mark on a blank pieces of paper." 

 26. However, even then the learned Advocate for the complainant-opposite party though raised his argument saying that the burden of proof of a case is obviously upon the complainant as per the provision of sections 101 and 103 of the Evidence Act. But that burden also included to prove the presumption as raised in the trial proceeding; however, in the instant case the complainant himself as well as the Court's below has avoided such act of burden of proving the case for making proper decision thereto. 

 27. Learned Advocate for the complainant opposite party has also raised other submissions to the effect that as per section 134 of the Evidence Act there requires no particular number of witness to prove the complainant's case. But the fact and the settled principle of law is that while the presumption of defective consideration is raised and that presumption has not been addressed properly that presumption certainly goes upon the complainant to prove the same again. In that case without supporting evidence a solitary witness is obviously not enough to proof the same. 

 28. However, as per the above noted enunciations of our apex Court, the burden of proof in certain cases also slightly goes to the accused-appellant who placed the presumption of defective consideration before the trial Court. To that extent our apex Court in the above cited decision, reported in 28 BLT (AD) 40 has categorically held that:— 

 "At the same time it is clear that bare denial of the passing of consideration apparently would not served the purpose of the accused, Something which is probable has to be brought on record for getting the burden of proof that shifted to the complainant. The burden of proof of the accused to disprove the presumption under section 118 and 138 of the Act is not so heavy. The preponderance of probability through direct or substantial evidence is sufficient enough to shift the onus to the complainant. 

 32. Thus, the above findings exactly relates with the facts and circumstances of the present case in hand and that is why, since the presumption raised about the defective consideration as written in the cheque in question, that has to be proved or disproved by the respective party and in proving their own case they have to be given a chance again to proof their own claim by producing their supporting respective evidence. And to that extent, this Court is inclined to send the case back to the appellate Court below who is the last Court of fact and has ignored the certain admitted facts of the case as well as the grounds taken and placed in appeal before him for deciding the said appeal and, as such, he is bound to discover the actual truth as behind the allegation brought in the case and then upon taking the additional evidence he has to make a decision thereto in accordance with law; however, keeping in mind the observations as made above by our apex Court and inasmuch as of the apex Court of this sub-continent. Hence, by the empowerment of section 439 read with section 375 inasmuch as following the provisions of section 423 & 428 of the CrPC this Court is inclined to send the case back to the appellate Court below to hold retrial of the case for taking decision upon enabling both the affected parties to place their additional evidence about to prove their own case as well as to prove and disprove the presumption raised herein.
